checkpoints: etcd assigns a Raft-ordered `createRevision` to a key at the moment it is written, and that value is already returned in the PUT response header (`putRes.header.revision`) rather than needing to be computed by the client.

Stamping a queue position with `Date.now()` on the client makes ordering depend on wall-clock time, and clocks on different machines can drift, so concurrent joins can leave two clients each believing they hold the head position.
`modRevision` (etcd3's `kv.mod_revision`) changes every time a key's value is written, while `createRevision` is fixed at the moment the key is first created and never changes afterward.

Sorting a queue by `modRevision` instead of `createRevision` causes the queue order to silently reshuffle whenever any ticket's value is updated, even though the ticket's actual join order never changed.

etcd supports server-side ordered retrieval — `getAll().prefix(prefix).sort("Create", "Ascend")` — which returns entries already sorted by creation order and removes the need for the client to compute or re-sort ordering itself.

A single-client demo has no concurrency and no mid-queue updates, so both the wall-clock-position bug and the modRevision-sort bug pass local testing while still being production-breaking under real concurrent load.

Client-computed ordering undermines the core reason to build a queue on etcd in the first place: etcd's Raft consensus already provides a total order across writes, so recomputing that order client-side reintroduces the exact race the system exists to remove.

A correct implementation keeps ticket ordering pinned to `createRevision` even when a ticket's value later changes, such as a progress field being updated mid-queue, since `createRevision` is immutable while `modRevision` moves with every subsequent write to that key.

Writing balance updates directly with `UPDATE account SET balance = $1 WHERE id = $2` and no corresponding `ledger_entry` row bypasses the ledger entirely, breaking the double-entry invariant `SUM(DEBIT) = SUM(CREDIT)`.

Once the ledger and the cached `account.balance` diverge this way, the invariant check exposed at `GET /api/invariant` starts reporting a mismatch that has nothing to do with an underlying bug — the reconciliation "fix" itself is what caused it.

Without a `ledger_entry`, nothing distinguishes an automated system correction from a customer genuinely moving that money, so replaying the event log makes the correction look as if it never happened.
Without a `reconciliation_run` row, there is no way to answer when reconciliation last ran, what drift it found, or what it fixed — the audit history a proper reconcile loop is expected to persist.

The correct fix is a compensating `ledger_entry` shaped like a real transfer: the delta computed as a `BigInt`, direction set to `DEBIT` or `CREDIT` depending on sign, and a `compensating: TRUE` flag marking it as an automated correction rather than customer activity.
The compensating ledger entry insert and the `account.balance` update must happen together inside a single transaction (`BEGIN`/`COMMIT`), never as a bare `UPDATE` issued outside of any ledger write.
A `reconciliation_run` row should be inserted alongside the fix, capturing the trigger, the drift count, and the fixes applied, so each correction is traceable to a specific run.

The fix can be verified by calling `GET /api/invariant` and confirming `balanced: true`, and by querying `ledger_entry WHERE compensating = TRUE` to see the correction appear as a flagged, run-linked row rather than an untraceable balance edit.

The invariant endpoint runs two full-table `SUM(amount)` aggregations — one for DEBIT, one for CREDIT — over the entire `ledger_entry` table on every call, so its cost is O(rows) and grows without bound as the ledger grows.

`ledger_entry` is append-only and immutable: rows written yesterday never change, so re-summing the whole table from scratch on every 30-second poll re-derives an answer that was already correct before, wasting work on settled history instead of just accounting for new rows.

The correct fix is turning the aggregate from something RECOMPUTED on read into something MAINTAINED on write — a `ledger_summary` table (or a Postgres materialized view) that holds the running `totalDebits`/`totalCredits` and is updated the moment a transfer happens, rather than a blind cache slapped in front of the existing query.

The running totals can be updated inline, inside the exact same `BEGIN…COMMIT` transaction that already inserts the debit/credit `ledger_entry` rows, so the summary can never drift out of sync with what was actually written — or updated asynchronously through a CDC stream, such as Debezium tailing the Postgres WAL, feeding a small consumer that applies each new row to the summary.

If a materialized view is used instead of a hand-maintained summary table, it needs a periodic job — for example a NestJS `@Cron()` task — to run `REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY` so the view stays reasonably current.

After the fix, `GET /invariant` becomes a single-row read like `SELECT totalDebits, totalCredits FROM ledger_summary`, which is O(1) regardless of whether `ledger_entry` holds thousands or billions of rows.

`account.balance` is already an example of this exact write-through-cache pattern, updated inline with every transfer, which is why per-account balance reads are already O(1); only the global invariant check was still doing the expensive full recompute.

Moving to an incrementally maintained total introduces a new risk — a bug in the increment logic or CDC consumer could silently drift from the truth — so a periodic authoritative full-table SUM, such as a nightly reconciliation job, must still run and alert loudly the moment it diverges from the cached totals, keeping the cheap O(1) check honest without paying its cost on every poll.

A nightly full scan that walks every account regardless of recent activity is bound by two independent constraints at once — the total account count and a single concurrency=1 worker draining the queue serially — so once the account base reaches billions, no amount of per-query speedup removes that ceiling; the bottleneck is architectural, not a slow SUM query.

Partitioning the account base (by id hash, by country, or by product line) into separate queues, each with its own worker, turns one serial walk over the entire dataset into many partitions reconciling in parallel, directly addressing the throughput ceiling.

An activity-driven filter — a CDC stream off the ledger table (e.g. Debezium), or a lighter mechanism like Postgres LISTEN/NOTIFY — lets a run skip accounts with no new activity since the last cut-off, instead of recomputing the ledger SUM for every account whether or not it changed since yesterday.

Partitioning and activity-driven filtering solve two different kinds of waste and are complementary rather than substitutes for each other: partitioning alone still re-sums every untouched account inside each partition, while filtering alone still funnels every matching account through a single worker per partition.

Keeping each partition's queue at concurrency=1 preserves the original safety property that no two workers can ever race on the same account and post two separate compensating entries for the same drift.

Reconciling against a single cut-off timestamp captured once at the start of a run, rather than an open-ended 'now', prevents a transaction still in flight from the external truth source from being mistaken for drift.

Introducing a CDC-driven path adds a new risk that the original full scan didn't have: a dropped or missed change event would silently hide real drift, so running a periodic full, unfiltered sweep alongside the activity-driven path (e.g. weekly) acts as a backstop that proves the filtered runs aren't missing anything.

Taking row locks in the order arguments happen to arrive in a request — first `fromAccountId`, then `toAccountId` — instead of a deterministic order makes the lock acquisition sequence depend on transfer direction, which is the actual root cause of an intermittent Postgres `deadlock detected` error, not anything wrong with the SQL itself.

When a transfer A→B and a concurrent transfer B→A both run `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` on the same two accounts in opposite orders, the A→B transaction locks A and then blocks waiting for B, while the B→A transaction locks B and then blocks waiting for A — each transaction ends up holding exactly the row the other one needs next, forming a classic ABBA cycle.

Postgres's deadlock detector recognizes this wait-for cycle and resolves it by aborting one of the two transactions with a `deadlock detected` error while letting the other proceed, which is why the failure surfaces as an intermittent 500 rather than a hang.

Single-direction transfers on a given account pair never trigger this deadlock because only one transaction is touching the pair at a time — the cycle only forms when two transactions traveling in opposite directions race on the same pair of accounts concurrently.

The fix is to make lock acquisition order independent of transfer direction by sorting the two account ids and always locking the smaller one first, ideally in a single query such as `SELECT ... FROM account WHERE id = ANY($1) ORDER BY id FOR UPDATE` with the id array pre-sorted.

Once both A→B and B→A requests are forced to acquire the same first row regardless of which way the transfer is going, the second transaction simply queues and waits behind the first instead of each grabbing a different row and forming a cycle, so the deadlock cannot occur.
Transfers between disjoint account pairs never contend on the same row, so imposing a deterministic lock order costs nothing in throughput — full parallelism is preserved for unrelated transfers.

The fix should be verified by firing many concurrent A→B and B→A transfers on the same account pair under load and confirming zero `deadlock detected` errors, correct final balances on both accounts, and an intact `SUM(DEBIT) = SUM(CREDIT)` invariant across the ledger.
